procedural_history.originating_court: Court of the Additional Sessions Judge, Burdwan, in Session Trial No. 1 of 1950
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated the 29th April, 1950, of the Court of the Additional Sessions Judge, Burdwan in Session Trial No. 1 of 1950.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant appealed to the High Court of Judicature at Calcutta. Das Gupta and Lahiri JJ. heard the case in Criminal Appeal No. 77 of 1950 and delivered a Judgment and Order dated the 21st of March, 1952. The High Court granted leave to appeal to the Supreme Court under Article 134(1)(c) of the Constitution of India, considering the point raised to be of considerable difficulty and fit for decision by the Supreme Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court after the High Court granted leave to appeal under Article 134(1)(c). The Union of India was allowed to intervene initially but their intervention became unnecessary as the appellant abandoned a point related to Section 269(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The appellant argued that the notification was in excess of the powers conferred on the State Government under section 269(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and that it denied the appellant equal protection of the laws under Article 14 of the Constitution.

issue.issue_text: Whether sanction under section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code was necessary for instituting proceedings against the appellant on charges of conspiracy and bribery.

facts: The appellant was facing proceedings on charges of conspiracy and bribery.
law: The Supreme Court considered the precedent set by two prior decisions from the Judicial Committee (Privy Council): H. H. B. Gill v. The King and Phanindra Chandra Neogy v. The King.
application: The Court found that the issue of whether a sanction under section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code was necessary for charges of conspiracy and bribery was already settled by these two previous cases.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the issue was already settled by the prior decisions of the Judicial Committee. Therefore, the question of whether a sanction was necessary must be answered in the negative, and the appellant's contention was rejected.

issue.issue_text: Whether there was a contravention of section 257 of the Criminal Procedure Code, resulting in a denial of a fair trial.

facts: The appellant was permitted by the Privy Council to raise the contention that there had been a contravention of section 257 of the Criminal Procedure Code during the trial.
law: Section 257 of the Criminal Procedure Code pertains to procedures that ensure a fair trial for the accused.
application: The Court, referencing "reasons already given" (which are not detailed in the provided text), directly addressed the issue.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court answered the question in the affirmative, holding that there was a contravention of section 257 of the Criminal Procedure Code, which resulted in a denial of a fair trial. On this ground, the Court set aside the appellant's conviction and allowed the appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the government notification withdrawing the right of trial by jury for particular cases was in excess of the powers conferred on the State Government under section 269(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

facts: The State Government issued a notification withdrawing the right of trial by jury for a specific set of cases known as the "Burdwan Test Relief Fraud cases".
This notification did not revoke the right to a jury trial for the underlying offences in general (e.g., sections 120-B, 467, 468 of the Indian Penal Code).
As a result, the individuals involved in these specific cases were denied a jury trial, while other persons accused of the same offences would still be entitled to one.
law: Section 269(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure empowers the State Government to direct that the trial of "all offences or of any particular class of offences" shall be by jury.
The section also grants the government the power to revoke or alter such an order.

The Court interpreted this to mean that the power of revocation is co-extensive with the power to grant, meaning it can only be applied to general classes of offences, not to individual cases or accused persons.
application: The Court found that Section 269(1) does not allow the government to create different trial procedures for people accused of the same offence but involved in different cases.
The impugned notification did not remove a class of offences from jury trial; instead, it singled out a specific group of individuals and cases.

By "picking out" a particular set of cases and denying those individuals the right to a jury trial while leaving the right intact for others committing the same offences, the government went beyond the scope of the power granted by the statute.
The Court contrasted this with previous valid notifications which were general in their terms and applied to categories of offences, irrespective of who committed them.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the government notification was in excess of the powers conferred by section 269(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Court held that the section only allows the government to grant or revoke jury trials for general classes of offences, not for particular cases or individuals. Therefore, the notification was void and inoperative.

issue.issue_text: Whether the notification, by depriving the appellant of the right to trial by jury while others charged with similar offences retained that right, denied the appellant equal protection of the laws under Article 14 of the Constitution.

facts: A government notification revoked the right to a trial by jury for a specific group of cases, referred to as the "Burdwan Test Relief Fraud cases".
This meant the appellant, who was part of this group, was to be tried by a Court of Session with the aid of assessors instead of a jury.

However, other individuals accused of the same or similar offenses (e.g., under sections 120-B, 420, 467 of the Penal Code) but not involved in this specific set of cases, retained their right to be tried by a jury.
law: Article 14 of the Constitution guarantees equal protection of the laws.
For a law or notification that creates a classification to be valid under Article 14, the classification must not be arbitrary.
The classification must be based on a "real and substantial distinction bearing a just and reasonable relation to the objects sought to be attained."
application: The Supreme Court found that the notification created an arbitrary classification by singling out a specific group of individuals and cases rather than applying to a general class of offenses.
The Court contrasted this with previous, valid notifications which had specified that all trials for certain *classes of offenses* in a district would be by jury, regardless of who the accused was.

The impugned notification, however, did not remove any offenses from the list of those triable by jury; instead, it denied the right to a jury trial to "certain individuals" (those in the Burdwan cases) while others accused of the very same offenses retained that right.

The Court rejected the High Court's reasoning that the complexity of evidence in these specific cases was a valid basis for classification, stating that the classification was "arbitrary and without any substantial basis" and had no reasonable relation to the objective.
By treating individuals accused of the same offenses differently based on their involvement in a particular named set of cases, the notification created an unconstitutional discrimination.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the notification contravened Article 14 of the Constitution. By arbitrarily denying the appellant the right to a trial by jury while others charged with the same offenses retained that right, the notification denied the appellant equal protection of the laws and was therefore void and inoperative.

issue.issue_text: Whether the trial of the appellant, which continued after the commencement of the Constitution (26th January, 1950) with the aid of assessors, was bad in law and vitiated.

facts: The appellant's trial began before the Constitution came into force on January 26, 1950, but continued after this date.
The trial was conducted by a Sessions Judge with the aid of assessors, based on a government notification issued in 1947.
The appellant argued that this procedure denied him the equal protection of laws guaranteed under Article 14 of the Constitution, which came into effect during his trial.
law: Article 14 of the Constitution guarantees equal protection of the laws.
A trial procedure that is inconsistent with Article 14 is unconstitutional and invalid.

Precedent established that it is not possible to convert a trial that began under a discriminatory procedure (like trial by assessors) into a non-discriminatory one (like trial by jury) midway through the proceedings.
If a discriminatory procedure cannot be separated from the rest of the trial, the entire trial is considered bad in law.
application: The Court determined that continuing the trial with assessors after the Constitution came into force was a procedure inconsistent with the provisions of Article 14.

This procedure was found to be prejudicial to the accused. The Court noted that if the assessors had been jurors and delivered their "not guilty" verdict, the appellant would likely have been acquitted.
The Court reasoned that it was impossible to change the trial from one with assessors to one with a jury after the Constitution became effective.

Citing previous cases, the Court held that since the discriminatory procedure was adopted from the beginning and could not be corrected later, the entire trial after January 26, 1950, had to be condemned as bad.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the trial of the appellant after January 26, 1950, with the aid of assessors was bad in law. Consequently, the Court quashed the trial, set aside the conviction, and directed that the appellant be set free.

respondent_arguments: The trial had started with the help of assessors before the Constitution came into force, and it was a good trial that cannot be said to be vitiated by the subsequent commencement of the Constitution.

cases.case_name: The State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar
cases.principle: A jury trial could not be revoked in respect of a particular case or a particular accused while in respect of other cases involving the same offences that order still remained in force.

Whether an enactment providing for special procedure for the trial of certain offences is or is not discriminatory and violates Article 14 of the Constitution must be determined in each case as it arises, and no general rule applicable to all cases can be laid down.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A law or government notification that provides for a special trial procedure for a particular case or accused person, while other persons accused of the same offense are tried under the general procedure, violates Article 14 of the Constitution if the classification is not based on a real and substantial distinction that bears a just and reasonable relation to the object of the law.
obiter: Whether an enactment providing for a special procedure for the trial of certain offences is discriminatory and violates Article 14 of the Constitution must be determined in each case as it arises, and no general rule applicable to all cases can be laid down.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the trial of the appellant was bad in law and the conviction must be set aside. This was because the government notification that withdrew the right to a jury trial for the appellant's specific case was invalid on two grounds. First, it exceeded the powers conferred by section 269(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code, which allows the government to specify trial by jury for classes of offences, but not to single out particular cases or accused persons for different treatment. Second, the notification was discriminatory and violated the equal protection clause of Article 14 of the Constitution. The classification of the appellant's case based on the 'mass of evidence' and potential length of the trial was found to be arbitrary and without a reasonable relation to the objective, as these features are common to many complex cases tried by jury. Since the trial continued with assessors under this unconstitutional procedure after the Constitution came into force, the entire proceeding was vitiated.
legal_tests_applied: For a classification to be valid under Article 14 of the Constitution, it must be based on some real and substantial distinction bearing a just and reasonable relation to the objects sought to be attained and cannot be made arbitrarily and without any substantial basis.

Section 269(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure empowers the State Government to direct that the trial of all offences or of any particular class of offences shall be by jury, but it does not empower the government to direct that the trial of a particular case or a particular accused person shall be conducted differently from others accused of the same offence.

An objection that goes to the very root of the jurisdiction of the Court is not a mere procedural irregularity curable under section 536 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and can be taken notice of at any stage.
why_appellant_lost: The reasoning for why the court rejected the appellant's argument on the issue of requiring sanction under section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code is not available in the provided text.
why_respondent_won: The reasoning for why the court found that sanction under section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code was not necessary is not available in the provided text.
policy_considerations: It would not advance the ends of justice if at this stage a fresh trial by jury is ordered in this case.

The memory of jurors, assessors, judges and of other persons who have to form their judgment on the facts of any case, can afford no reasonable basis for a classification and for denial of equal protection of the laws.
